entries.english:
Ancillary plaintiff/applicant/intervener: Wilhelm von Lichtenstein zu Memmelsdorf and Heilgersdorf (also spelled Heiligsdorf and Heiligersdorf in the file), defendant at first instance. Ancillary defendants/interveners: Bishop Johann Gottfried of Bamberg and Würzburg; and Valtin Schad, Valtin Hoffmann, and David Murmann, citizens and council members of Seßlach, as guardians of the four children of Hans Schneider of Heilgersdorf—Adam, Jakob, Eva, and Kunigunda Schneider. Valtin Schad, together with Heinz Praußer and Kaspar Schleifenheimer, citizens of Seßlach, was plaintiff before the imperial provincial court of the Duchy of Franconia; with Valtin Hoffmann and David Murmann he was plaintiff before the prince-bishopric of Würzburg’s court and chancery court. Plaintiff’s attorney: Dr. Christoph Stauber (1618). Defendants’ attorney: Dr. Christian Schröter (1618).

Contemporary description: appeal concerning the estate of Hans Schneider. The dispute concerned jurisdiction over a guardianship.

At first instance, when Hans Schneider of Heilgersdorf remarried in early 1616, he assigned 1,600 gulden as an advance inheritance (prelegatum) to his children from his first marriage and, with Wilhelm von Lichtenstein’s consent, entrusted citizens of Seßlach with the care of this money. After Schneider died in autumn 1616, they unsuccessfully sought appointment as guardians and delivery of the estate. In mid-November 1616 they also relinquished their guardianship over the advance inheritance. Wilhelm von Lichtenstein then sent the children to Coburg to be raised, had an estate inventory prepared, and took custody at his castle of a chest containing bonds, valuables, and cash worth about 4,500 gulden. In mid-December 1616, acting for Nikolaus Schneider and Hans Schubart, citizens of Ummerstadt, the imperial provincial court of the Duchy of Franconia issued an order requiring Lichtenstein to deliver the entire estate to the curators. When he retained the chest and began selling livestock from the estate, Valtin Schad and two fellow citizens obtained a provincial-court mandate in mid-February 1617. In mid-April he asked for his two co-guardians to be reinstated. In mid-May 1617, by a judgment in default, the provincial court imposed on Lichtenstein the threatened penalty of 100 gulden. At the guardians’ request, the prince-bishopric’s court and chancery court at Würzburg issued an enforcement mandate in mid-November 1617; in early March 1618 it imposed the reserved penalty of 200 Reichstaler and issued stricter enforcement orders.

Lichtenstein appealed the May 1617 and March 1618 judgments to the Reichskammergericht. He argued that, as a member of the Baunach knightly canton, he was exempt from the jurisdiction of both the provincial court and the prince-bishop’s court. His superior guardianship authority, he said, entitled him to appoint and swear in guardians, require inventories, and audit accounts. He accused the guardians of making false statements: they had been appointed caretakers of the advance inheritance, but not guardians because they refused to provide security; the chest had not been removed from Seßlach but had always been at Heilgersdorf; and the two Saxon-Coburg subjects from Ummerstadt had denied both before the official at Heldburg and before the Coburg government that they had ever appealed to the provincial court. Instead, two Seßlach citizens with no connection to the matter had appeared there. The bishop argued that the amount in dispute fell below the 1,000-gulden minimum for appeal, that Lichtenstein had bypassed the court and chancery court as the appellate instance, and that his appeal was late. The bishop maintained that Würzburg’s judicial privileges subjected Lichtenstein to the provincial court’s jurisdiction and that he had to deliver the estate to guardians confirmed by that court. The recorded proceedings before the Reichskammergericht began in 1618 and are dated 1618–1623 (the register records 1618–1628).

The file includes: Emperor Rudolf II’s 1586 appellate privilege for the bishopric in cases with a value in dispute up to 1,000 gulden (Q 11); privileges and confirmations issued for the Bishopric of Würzburg by Emperors Henry V (1120), Maximilian I (1510), and Charles V (1532), and, in printed form, by Frederick I (1168) and Charles V (1534 and 1545), concerning the grant of judicial authority in the Duchy of Franconia, annulment of adverse privileges, and protection against prescription arising during the Reformation (Q 12–14, 18–20); fief charters issued by Emperors Charles IV (1372), Frederick III (1457), Maximilian I (1496), and Matthias (1613) (Q 15–17, 21); a schedule of cases involving nobles before the imperial provincial court of Franconia in 1499–1534, 1550–1554, 1560–1563, and 1570–1573 (Q 22); the provincial-court file (no. 26), including an inventory of the livestock, equipment, hay, and wood Wilhelm von Lichtenstein sold from the Schneider estate; and the guardians’ sworn guardianship oath (Q 30). It also includes Emperor Rudolf II’s privileges for the Franconian Imperial Knighthood against reduction to the status of territorial subjects, confirming an inserted privilege of Emperor Ferdinand I of 1559, and against the imposition of sequestrations (1609; Q 36–37).

Extracts from the Würzburg Rotulus (see order no. 1565), Q 41b: King Frederick III’s 1442 command to pay homage to Gotfried von Limpurg, administrator of the bishopric, authenticated in 1442 by Abbots Karl II of St. Burkard and Berthold of St. Stephan in Würzburg; the related 1442 letter to the mayor and council of Würzburg from Wilhelm von Henneberg-Schleusingen, Georg von Henneberg-Aschach, (Wilhelm von) Castell, (Konrad von) Weinsberg, Herman von Schwarzenberg, Lorenz von Ostheim, Eucharius von Heßberg, Bernhard von Schaumberg, Siegmund von Thüngen, Adolf Marschall (von Ostheim), Caspar von Bibra, Karl von Bastheim, and Konrad von Klingenberg (nos. 17–18); extracts from agreements among Bishops Johann II, Johann III, Rudolf II, and Konrad II, the cathedral chapter, and the nobility of the Bishopric of Würzburg, dated 1412, 1456, 1467, and 1525, the last confirmed by Emperor Charles V in 1526 (nos. 19–22); the 1485 undertaking by Michael and Sigmund the Younger von Schwarzenberg, father and son, to hold Stephansberg Castle in fief solely from the bishopric, with the consent of Sigmund the Elder and Hans von Schwarzenberg, father and son (no. 23); and extracts from letters recognizing the bishopric’s territorial lordship: in 1485 by Berthold, Count and Elector of Mainz; Friedrich; Georg, Teutonic Order commander at Mergentheim; Heinrich, cathedral canon at Strasbourg; Otto von Henneberg-Aschach; and Margaretha, Countess of Henneberg-Schleusingen, née Duchess of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel; and in 1535 by Count Wolfgang of Hohenlohe (nos. 24–28).

Appendix volume to the Würzburg pleading of exceptions and proofs (see order no. 1565), Q 41c: an extract from Bishop Johann III’s confirmation of the 1458 testament issued by Michael the Elder von Schwarzenberg after Abbot Mauritius III of the Würzburg Scottish monastery, acting as papal commissioner, had recognized his marriage to Ursula Frankengrüner (no. 29); the 1477 judgment of the imperial provincial court of Franconia in Philipp von Weinsberg’s forfeiture suit against Reinhard Truchseß (von Baldersheim) concerning male fiefs at Unterbalbach, Reichelsburg (called Reigelberg in the file), and Burgerroth (no. 30); an extract from the 1483 judgment of the imperial commissioners Elector Ernst and Duke Albrecht of Saxony in the dispute between Bishop Rudolf II of Würzburg and Count Friedrich von Henneberg-Aschach, together with the mayor, village headmen, and community of Linden, over an appeal from the imperial provincial court (no. 31); an extract from the 1500 settlement between Bishop Rudolf II and Valentin von Bibra concerning redemption of the prince-bishopric’s share in Irmelshausen fortress, before the arbitrators Albrecht von Bibra, cathedral canon at Bamberg and Würzburg and provost of St. Johann zu Neumünster, and Bartholomäus von Herbilstadt (no. 32); the 1489 acknowledgment by Christoph Fuchs (von Bimbach), prince-bishopric of Würzburg marshal and official at Zabelstein, that he had accepted Götz von Füllbach as a prince-bishopric servant and vassal (no. 33); an extract from the 1489 order of Bishop Rudolf II and Count Otto von Henneberg-Aschach on proceedings against Hermann the Elder and Hermann the Younger Riedesel, father and son, after their declaration of feud against the count (no. 34); and letters from Lorenz von Rosenberg to Bishop Melchior of Würzburg in 1550 and Hans Eucharius von Rosenberg to Bishop Julius in 1574 concerning complaints brought before the Reichskammergericht by Joachim von Niedeck and Zaisolph von Rosenberg respectively (see order no. 10946), together with the related 1551 judgment (nos. 35–40). Also included are guardianship accounts, submitted before the respective chief guardians Wolf, Erhard, and Martin von Lichtenstein, for the guardianships over the children of Kunz Linck of Bischwind, Wolf, Hans, and Klaus Linck, and Margaretha Biber, daughter of Klaus Biber of Dürrnhof, 1569–1600 (Q 46–50).

Contents note: The register gives 1618 as the start of proceedings. The listed prior instances are the imperial provincial court of the Duchy of Franconia at Würzburg (1617) and the prince-bishopric of Würzburg’s court and chancery court (1617). It also indexes the von Bibra family (as arbitrators); the imperial provincial court of the Duchy of Franconia under Würzburg’s prince-bishop; the von Herbilstadt family (as arbitrators); the Ernestine and Albertine lines of the Duchy/Electorate of Saxony, including Elector Ernst (d. 1486) and Albrecht the Bold (d. 1500); and the prince-bishopric of Würzburg’s court and chancery court.
